findings.claim: “When Benedick arrives, the merry war begins in earnest… Beatrice calls Benedick “a disease” and compares him to food she finds unappetising.”
findings.truth: The “disease” line is spoken to the Messenger BEFORE Benedick enters (“he will hang upon him like a disease”, of Claudio). After he enters, Beatrice's opening shot is “I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick: nobody marks you.” The “food” line is Beatrice's “such meet food to feed it [Disdain] as Signior Benedick” — Benedick feeds her disdain; it is not food she finds unappetising.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1519 l.263 (Messenger scene, before the entry at l.283) and ll.318, 326-327 (Act 1 Scene 1)

findings.claim: Flashcard [2]: “What does Beatrice call Benedick on his arrival?” → “'A disease' — she compares him to unappetising food in rapid stichomythia.”
findings.truth: Same error as F1: the line precedes his arrival and is addressed to the Messenger, and the food reading is wrong.

findings.claim: “Took up a beggar’s issue at my gate”
findings.truth: The text reads “Took up a beggar’s issue at my gates” (plural). One-letter misquote; not mark-affecting, and a fix would force a re-narration of the block.

findings.claim: “He visits the tomb and delivers a song of mourning: “Pardon, goddess of the night, / Those that slew thy virgin knight.””
findings.truth: Claudio does not sing. He hangs and reads the epitaph (“Done to death by slanderous tongues”), then orders “Now, music, sound, and sing your solemn hymn.” The hymn “Pardon, goddess of the night” is headed “Song.” and is sung by the musicians (Balthasar in most editions), not by Claudio. Attributing the song to Claudio is a speaker error a student would repeat in an essay.

findings.claim: Flashcard [5]: “Which line opens Claudio's mourning song at the tomb?” → “'Pardon, goddess of the night.'”
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F4. The song is not Claudio's; Claudio reads the epitaph and calls for the hymn.

findings.claim: “our watch, sir, have indeed comprehended two auspicious persons”
findings.truth: The word is “aspicious”, not “auspicious”. This matters here because the sentence is teaching the line AS a malapropism: “auspicious” is a real English word, so the misquote blunts the very point being made (“aspicious” for “suspicious”).

findings.claim: “Dogberry consistently uses the wrong words: … “remember that I am an ass” (he means they should remember he is a respectable officer).”
findings.truth: “Remember that I am an ass” is not a malapropism at all — every word is the one Dogberry intends. Conrade has just called him an ass, and Dogberry wants the insult put on the official record as evidence (“O that he were here to write me down an ass!”). He is not substituting a wrong word, and he does not mean “remember I am a respectable officer”. A student using this as a malapropism example, with this gloss, would be marked as misreading the scene.

findings.claim: “Benedick’s final words to Don Pedro … echo the play’s opening pattern: just as Antonio was melancholic in The Merchant of Venice, Don Pedro stands alone at the end of the festivities.”
findings.truth: The MoV Antonio comparison is a fair critical analogy, but “echo the play’s opening pattern” is unsupported — Much Ado opens festively, not with a melancholic figure. There is also a confusion risk: Much Ado has its own Antonio (Leonato’s brother), so a student may attach the melancholy to the wrong character. Not worth a narration-rippling edit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1519 ll.134-330 (Act 1 Scene 1, festive opening); Antonio of Much Ado at ll.632ff

findings.claim: “She [Hero] has fewer lines than any other major character.”
findings.truth: False. Counted over the whole play, Hero speaks 130 printed lines / 987 words; Don John — the villain, and one of the seven characters this very lesson analyses — speaks 92 lines / 908 words. The Friar (82 lines) also speaks less. The true and usable point is that Hero speaks less than half as much as Beatrice (987 words vs 2,359).
findings.evidence: Speaker-attributed word/line counts over Gutenberg #1519 ll.132-4700: BENEDICK 440/4459, DON PEDRO 275/2455, LEONATO 321/2664, CLAUDIO 273/2074, BEATRICE 227/2359, DOGBERRY 150/1561, HERO 130/987, DON JOHN 92/908

findings.claim: KC [3]: “Hero has _____ lines than any other major character in the play”, keyed to “fewer”.
findings.truth: The answer key marks a false statement as correct (see F9). Re-anchoring the comparison to Beatrice makes “fewer” true and keeps the key index unchanged.

findings.claim: Flashcard [8]: “She has fewest lines, does not choose her husband, cannot defend herself, and speaks nothing on restoration.”
findings.truth: Two errors. “Fewest lines” is false (F9). “Speaks nothing on restoration” is also false — Hero speaks on being unveiled: “One Hero died defil’d, but I do live, / And surely as I live, I am a maid.”
findings.evidence: Counts as in F9; Gutenberg #1519 l.4505 (Act 5 Scene 4)

findings.claim: Mark scheme [3]: “Hero has fewer lines than any major character.”
findings.truth: The same false superlative as F9, restated in a mark scheme students read while self-marking.

findings.claim: Across all 7 lessons, 42 practice questions carry three type labels: “30+4 marks — Shakespeare Essay” (18), “8 marks — Extract Analysis” (12) and “4 marks — Quote Analysis” (12). The band ladders read 25-30 / 19-24 / 13-18 / 7-12 / 3-6 / 1-2.
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section A sets exactly ONE question on the play: an extract printed on the paper plus the whole text, 30 marks + 4 SPaG, closed book. There is no 8-mark extract question and no 4-mark quote question on this paper, and several of the questions so labelled are not extract questions at all (e.g. L1 Q4 on honour ‘refer to at least two characters’). The AQA Shakespeare mark scheme also uses six equal 5-mark levels (26-30 / 21-25 / 16-20 / 11-15 / 6-10 / 1-5), not the ladders printed here. Two further shape problems: L4 Q1 names a 3-line extract (‘Sweet Prince, you learn me noble thankfulness’ to ‘rotten orange’, ll.2921-2923), far too short for a 30-mark answer, and L3 Q1 names a ~150-line span (ll.1661-1814), far too long. OPTIONS: (a) route the whole unit to the existing 190-relabel + 178-band-ladder workstream, which is what I recommend — relabelling forces the mark schemes to be rewritten too, so it is not a surgical edit; (b) fix labels only and leave mismatched band descriptors, which I do not recommend; (c) leave as is. The spec markdown carries no level descriptors, so the ladder claim rests on the AQA mark scheme, not on an in-repo source.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md ll.222-243 (Paper 1: 1h45, 64 marks, Section A one question, extract + whole play) and l.217 (all assessments closed book); Gutenberg #1519 ll.2921-2923, 1661-1814

summary: Seven lessons checked against Gutenberg #1519 and the 8702 spec; 13 findings, 9 edited. The real damage is concentrated in L5 and L6: Claudio is credited with singing the tomb hymn he only calls for, and Hero is claimed to have fewer lines than any other major character when Don John has fewer — a claim the knowledge-check key, a flashcard and a mark scheme all repeat. Quotation accuracy is otherwise high: every other quoted line in the unit verified verbatim against the text, including speaker, act and scene.
